lesson.title: Nothing Is Something: Understanding None
lesson.summary: None is Python's built-in way of representing the deliberate absence of a value, distinct from zero, an empty string, or False, and it is what a function silently returns when it does not return anything else.
lesson.body:
Every value in Python belongs to a type: 5 is an int, "hi" is a str, [1, 2] is a list. But sometimes a program needs to represent that there is no meaningful value at all, not zero, not an empty string, just nothing. Python has exactly one value for this job: None. Its type is called NoneType, and None is the only value that type ever has. Checking type(None) in an interpreter confirms this: it reports <class 'NoneType'>, a type built specifically to hold a single, unique placeholder.

None is easy to confuse with other "empty-looking" values, but it is not the same as 0, "", or an empty list. Those are real values within their own types that happen to be falsy in a boolean context. None is a separate concept: absence itself. For this reason, Python code checks for None using is, not ==. Writing if result is None reads as "is result the absence-of-a-value object", which is exactly the question being asked, and it also avoids subtle bugs where a custom object's __eq__ method could make == behave unexpectedly. This distinction matters in practice: writing if not result treats None the same as 0, an empty string, and an empty list, since all of those are falsy, so it can silently swallow a legitimate result of 0 as if nothing were returned at all. Writing if result is None avoids that trap entirely by checking specifically for the None object, not for falsiness in general.

None connects directly to return values. Every function in Python returns something, even if the function body never writes the word return. If control reaches the end of a function without hitting a return statement, or if a bare return is used with no expression after it, Python automatically returns None. This is not an error; it is the default. Consider this function with a missing case:

def get_grade(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"

result = get_grade(65)
print(result)

Tracing this: get_grade(65) checks 65 >= 90, which is False, then 65 >= 80, which is also False. Neither branch runs, there is no else, and the function body simply ends. Python does not raise an error for this; it returns None automatically. So result is bound to None, and print(result) displays None on screen, not an empty line and not an error. This is one of the most common early bugs: a function looks like it always returns a letter grade, but for low scores it silently returns nothing at all, and the bug only surfaces later when code tries to use result as if it were a string.

Because None shows up automatically whenever a function is incomplete, it doubles as a useful signal. Many built-in and library functions return None on purpose to mean "nothing found" or "no result", such as a dictionary's .get() method when a key is missing, or the .append() method on a list, which mutates the list in place and returns None precisely to remind you it was not meant to be used as an expression. Recognizing None, and knowing that it is a specific, single, checkable value rather than just an absence of output, is what lets you reason correctly about what a function actually gives back.
